questions.stem: In Young's double slit experiment, light passing through two narrow slits forms a pattern of bright and dark bands on a screen. Why is this evidence for the wave model of light?
options: The bands show that light is made of particles that pass through one slit or the other
The bands show that light travels in straight lines from each slit to the screen
The bands come from light reflecting off the edges of the slits onto the screen
The bands come from constructive and destructive interference, which only waves show
questions.explanation: Bright bands form where waves from the two slits arrive in phase and dark bands where they arrive out of phase. A particle model with straight-line paths predicts just two bright strips behind the slits, not a series of evenly spaced bands.

questions.stem: In a double slit pattern, what produces a dark band at a point on the screen?
options: Light from only one of the slits reaching that point on the screen
Waves from the two slits arriving half a wavelength out of phase
Waves from the two slits arriving exactly in phase with each other
Light from both slits being blocked by the barrier between them
questions.explanation: A dark band forms where the path difference from the two slits is an odd number of half wavelengths, so the waves arrive out of phase and cancel by destructive interference. Waves arriving in phase reinforce, giving a bright band.

questions.stem: Light is described as an electromagnetic wave. What does this mean?
options: It is a vibration of an invisible medium that fills all of space
It is a stream of electrons travelling through space at high speed
It is a pressure wave that can only travel through transparent matter
It consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields travelling at c
questions.explanation: Light is a transverse wave of electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, moving through a vacuum at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. It needs no medium, so it travels through empty space.

questions.stem: As the temperature of a black body increases, how does the spectrum of radiation it emits change?
options: The peak stays at the same wavelength and only the intensity increases
The peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the total intensity increases
The peak moves to longer wavelengths and the total intensity increases
The peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the total intensity decreases
questions.explanation: Wien's law, λmax = b/T, shows the peak wavelength is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature, so hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths. The intensity at every wavelength also rises, so the total emitted power increases. This is why a heated metal glows red, then orange, then white.

questions.stem: Three stars appear red, yellow and blue. Treating them as black bodies, which is the hottest?
options: The red star
The yellow star
All three have the same temperature
The blue star
questions.explanation: By Wien's law, λmax = b/T, a hotter body peaks at a shorter wavelength. Blue light has the shortest wavelength of the three colours, so the blue star is the hottest and the red star is the coolest.

questions.stem: Classical wave theory predicted that a black body should emit ever more intense radiation at shorter and shorter wavelengths. How did Planck explain the observed spectrum instead?
options: Energy is emitted in discrete quanta of size E = hf
Short-wavelength light travels more slowly inside a black body
Black bodies absorb all ultraviolet light and re-emit it as heat
Radiation is emitted continuously, but only at visible wavelengths
questions.explanation: Planck proposed that energy is emitted and absorbed in packets of E = hf. High-frequency quanta need a lot of energy, so few are emitted, and the intensity falls at short wavelengths, matching experiment. This quantisation was the first step towards quantum theory.

questions.stem: A star has a surface temperature of 5800 K. At what wavelength does its emission peak? Use b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K.
questions.explanation: λmax = b/T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 5800 ≈ 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, which is 500 nm, in the visible range. Multiplying b by T gives 17 m, and dividing T by b gives 2.0 × 10⁶ m.

questions.stem: The emission from a hot star peaks at 290 nm. What is its surface temperature? Use b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K.
questions.explanation: T = b/λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁴ K. Converting 290 nm as 2.90 × 10⁻¹⁰ m gives 1.0 × 10⁷ K, and dividing the wavelength by b gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ K.

questions.stem: Treated as a black body, Earth's surface has an average temperature of about 288 K. At what wavelength does its emission peak, and in which part of the spectrum? Use b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K.
options: 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, in the ultraviolet
1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, in the ultraviolet
5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, in the visible
1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, in the infrared
questions.explanation: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 288 ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m, or 10 µm. That is much longer than visible wavelengths (about 4 × 10⁻⁷ to 7 × 10⁻⁷ m), so it is in the infrared. Ultraviolet wavelengths are shorter than visible light, not longer.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 450 nm? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by λ gives 1.5 × 10⁻²⁷, which is the photon's momentum, not its energy. The other two values come from converting nanometres wrongly.

questions.stem: The wavelength of a beam of light is doubled. What happens to the energy of each photon?
options: It doubles
It falls to a quarter
It stays the same
It halves
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ, so photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength; doubling λ halves the energy of each photon. The brightness of the beam depends on how many photons arrive each second, not on the energy of each one.

questions.stem: The work function of a metal is:
options: the energy of the photons of light shone onto the metal
the total energy of all the free electrons in the metal
the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from its surface
the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted from it
questions.explanation: The work function W is the least energy a photon must give an electron to free it from the surface. It is related to the threshold frequency by W = hf₀. Any photon energy beyond W becomes the kinetic energy of the photoelectron.

questions.stem: Light shines on a metal, and no electrons are emitted however bright the light is made. What does this show?
options: The light is above the threshold frequency, so it passes through the metal
The frequency is below the threshold frequency, so each photon has too little energy
The light is not intense enough to supply the work function to any electrons
The metal's electrons need to absorb energy for longer before escaping
questions.explanation: Each electron absorbs a single photon, so emission depends on photon energy, hf, not on intensity. Below the threshold frequency no photon has enough energy to overcome the work function, and making the light brighter only sends more of these photons. The wave model wrongly predicted that brighter light would eventually eject electrons.

questions.stem: Why are photoelectrons emitted with no measurable delay, even when the light is very dim?
options: Dim light is made of photons with higher energy each
The electrons slowly store energy until they can escape
Dim light still carries a large total energy each second
Each electron absorbs one photon's energy all at once
questions.explanation: In the photon model, an electron gains all of a photon's energy in a single interaction, so it can escape at once if hf exceeds the work function. A wave model predicted that in dim light electrons would need time to accumulate enough energy, but no delay is observed.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 250 nm falls on a metal with a work function of 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: The photon energy is hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Then Ek = hf − W = 7.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The value 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is the photon energy alone, and adding the work function gives 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁸ J.

questions.stem: A photoelectron leaves a metal surface with a kinetic energy of 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its speed? Use electron mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
options: 2.4 × 10¹¹ m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Ek = ½mv², so v = √(2Ek/m) = √(2 × 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) ≈ 4.9 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 2.4 × 10¹¹, which would be faster than light, and leaving out the factor of 2 gives 3.5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: A metal has a work function of 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its threshold frequency? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
options: 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz
1.8 × 10¹⁵ Hz
questions.explanation: From W = hf₀, f₀ = W/h = 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Dividing h by W gives 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁵, and multiplying them gives 2.5 × 10⁻⁵², neither of which is a sensible frequency for light.

questions.stem: Graphs of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against light frequency are drawn for metals X and Y. The lines are parallel, and Y's line crosses the frequency axis at a higher frequency. What can be concluded?
options: Y has the larger work function, and Y's gradient is larger than X's
Both metals have the same work function but different threshold frequencies
Y has the larger work function, and both gradients equal Planck's constant
Y has the smaller work function, and both gradients equal Planck's constant
questions.explanation: Ek = hf − W, so every metal gives a straight line of gradient h, which is why the lines are parallel. The frequency-axis intercept is the threshold frequency f₀, and W = hf₀, so the metal with the higher intercept has the larger work function. Threshold frequency and work function always rise together.

questions.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz needs a stopping voltage of 1.2 V. What stopping voltage is needed for light of 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz on the same metal? Use h/e = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s.
questions.explanation: Ek = eV, so V = (h/e)f − W/e. The change in frequency of 2.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz changes V by 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 2.0 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 0.83 V, so the new stopping voltage is 1.2 − 0.83 ≈ 0.37 V. Scaling 1.2 V in proportion to the frequency gives 0.90 V, but the line does not pass through the origin.

questions.stem: A student measures the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons as 0.50 eV for light of 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and 1.33 eV for light of 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is the threshold frequency of the metal?
options: 7.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz
4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz
6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
1.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz
questions.explanation: The gradient is (1.33 − 0.50)/(2.0 × 10¹⁴) ≈ 4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s, which is Planck's constant in eV s. Extending the line down to Ek = 0 drops the frequency by 0.50/4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵ ≈ 1.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz, so f₀ ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz. 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz still gives photoelectrons, so it must be above the threshold.

questions.stem: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, a very few alpha particles bounced back at large angles. What did this show?
options: The atom's positive charge is spread evenly through a large sphere
Electrons occupy fixed orbits at particular distances from the nucleus
Gold atoms are packed so tightly that there is no space between them
The atom's positive charge and most of its mass are in a tiny, dense nucleus
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space, but the rare large deflections needed a concentrated positive charge to repel them. Rutherford concluded that the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny nucleus. Fixed electron orbits were Bohr's later addition.

questions.stem: What was the main problem with Rutherford's model of electrons orbiting a nucleus?
options: It placed the positive charge of the atom in the electrons instead of the nucleus
It predicted that atoms should emit light only at a few specific wavelengths
Orbiting electrons accelerate, so classically they should radiate energy and spiral in
It could not explain why most alpha particles passed straight through the foil
questions.explanation: An electron in circular orbit is accelerating, and classical electromagnetism says accelerating charges radiate. It should therefore lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, emitting a continuous spectrum, so stable atoms with line spectra could not be explained. Bohr's model was proposed to fix this.

questions.stem: How did Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom differ from Rutherford's?
options: Electrons are embedded in a sphere of positive charge, with no nucleus at all
Electrons can orbit at any distance and radiate energy continuously as they move
The nucleus orbits the electrons, which stay at rest at the centre of the atom
Electrons occupy only certain allowed orbits, and emit light only when they jump between them
questions.explanation: Bohr kept Rutherford's nucleus but proposed stationary states: orbits with quantised angular momentum, mvr = nh/2π, in which electrons do not radiate. A photon is emitted or absorbed only when an electron moves between levels, with energy equal to the difference between them.

questions.stem: How does Bohr's model explain why hydrogen emits light only at specific wavelengths?
options: The electron emits light continuously, but only some wavelengths escape the atom
The nucleus vibrates at a few natural frequencies and emits light at them
Each photon's energy equals the difference between two allowed energy levels
Each photon's energy equals the total energy of the electron in its orbit
questions.explanation: Electrons can only have the energies of the allowed levels, so when an electron drops from one to another, the photon carries away exactly the difference, E = hf = hc/λ. With only certain differences possible, only certain wavelengths appear, giving a line spectrum.

questions.stem: Which was a limitation of Bohr's model of the atom?
options: It could not explain the wavelengths of the lines in hydrogen's spectrum
It placed nearly all of the atom's mass in its electrons
It had no way to explain why atoms absorb light
It could not predict the spectra of atoms with more than one electron
questions.explanation: Bohr's model successfully predicted the wavelengths of hydrogen's spectral lines, but it failed for atoms with two or more electrons, and it gave no reason for its quantisation rule. Later quantum mechanics replaced it.

questions.stem: Use the Rydberg equation to find the wavelength emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2. Use R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.
options: 122 nm
656 nm
365 nm
103 nm
questions.explanation: 1/λ = R(1/nf² − 1/ni²) = 1.097 × 10⁷ × (1/4 − 1/9) ≈ 1.52 × 10⁶ m⁻¹, so λ ≈ 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m = 656 nm, a red line in the Balmer series. Leaving out the 1/9 term gives 365 nm, and 103 nm and 122 nm are the 3 → 1 and 2 → 1 transitions.

questions.stem: Hydrogen emits a visible line at 486 nm, from a transition ending on n = 2. Use the Rydberg equation, with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, to find the starting level.
questions.explanation: 1/λ = 1/(4.86 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 2.06 × 10⁶ m⁻¹, so 1/4 − 1/ni² = 2.06 × 10⁶ / 1.097 × 10⁷ ≈ 0.188. Then 1/ni² ≈ 0.0625 = 1/16, so ni = 4. The 3 → 2 transition gives the longer 656 nm line.

questions.stem: Electron transitions in hydrogen that end on the n = 1 level produce the Lyman series. In which part of the spectrum are these lines?
options: Infrared
Radio
Ultraviolet
Visible
questions.explanation: Transitions down to n = 1 involve the largest energy gaps in hydrogen, at least 10.2 eV, so the photons have short wavelengths, 122 nm and below, in the ultraviolet. Transitions ending on n = 2 give the Balmer series, several of which are visible.

questions.stem: A hydrogen atom has its electron in the n = 4 level. How many different photon energies could be emitted as the electron returns to the ground state by any route?
questions.explanation: The possible transitions are 4 → 3, 4 → 2, 4 → 1, 3 → 2, 3 → 1 and 2 → 1, giving six different photon energies. Counting only the direct jumps from n = 4 gives 3. Each transition gives one spectral line.

questions.stem: Hydrogen's energy levels are −13.6 eV (n = 1), −3.40 eV (n = 2), −1.51 eV (n = 3) and −0.85 eV (n = 4). Which photon could be absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state?
questions.explanation: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly matches a jump from the ground state: 13.6 − 1.51 ≈ 12.1 eV takes the electron to n = 3. 3.40 eV and 11.0 eV match no gap from n = 1. 1.89 eV is the 3 → 2 gap, which a ground-state atom cannot use.

questions.stem: In Bohr's model, the electron in hydrogen's lowest orbit has radius 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using mvr = nh/2π with n = 1, what is its speed? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and electron mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
questions.explanation: v = nh/(2πmr) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (2π × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹) ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Leaving out the 2π gives 1.4 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹, and multiplying by 2π instead of dividing gives 8.6 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: Using nλ = 2πr, how is an electron's de Broglie wavelength related to the radius r of the n = 3 orbit in Bohr's model?
options: λ = 2πr
λ = r/3
λ = 2πr/3
λ = 6πr
questions.explanation: Three whole de Broglie wavelengths fit around the orbit's circumference, so 3λ = 2πr and λ = 2πr/3. Multiplying by 3 instead of dividing gives 6πr. Using r instead of the circumference gives r/3.

questions.stem: How did de Broglie's matter waves explain Bohr's rule that only certain orbits are allowed?
options: Electron waves travel faster in larger orbits, so only the smallest orbit is stable
Electron waves spread out and cancel, so electrons stay in the nucleus between jumps
An electron wave must have the same wavelength as the light the atom emits
Only orbits whose circumference fits a whole number of electron wavelengths form standing waves
questions.explanation: If an electron behaves as a wave of wavelength λ = h/p, a stable orbit must fit a whole number of wavelengths around it, nλ = 2πr, forming a standing wave. Substituting λ = h/mv gives mvr = nh/2π, which is exactly Bohr's quantisation condition.

questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a proton moving at 2.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹? Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and proton mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2.0 × 10⁵) ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻¹² m. Dividing the momentum by h gives 5.0 × 10¹¹ m, the reciprocal of the correct answer.

questions.stem: A 0.16 kg cricket ball moves at 40 m s⁻¹. Why is no wave behaviour ever observed for it?
options: Its de Broglie wavelength is so large that it spreads beyond the ground
Waves are only produced by charged particles, and the ball is neutral
Its de Broglie wavelength, about 10⁻³⁴ m, is far too small to diffract
It has no de Broglie wavelength, because it is not a subatomic particle
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.16 × 40) ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³⁴ m, vastly smaller than any gap or obstacle, so no diffraction or interference can be seen. Every moving object has a de Broglie wavelength; the effect is only noticeable for tiny masses such as electrons.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches evidence with the model of light it supports?
options: Double slit interference supports waves; the photoelectric effect supports particles
Double slit interference supports particles; the photoelectric effect supports waves
Black-body radiation supports waves; double slit interference supports particles
The photoelectric effect and double slit interference both support waves
questions.explanation: Interference and diffraction, as in the double slit experiment, are wave behaviours. The photoelectric effect, with its threshold frequency and no time delay, needs light to arrive in quanta, as does Planck's explanation of black-body radiation. Light needs both models, which is wave-particle duality.

questions.stem: In a double slit experiment, the light is made so dim that photons pass through one at a time. Each lands as a single dot, but after many photons an interference pattern builds up. What does this show?
options: Light behaves as a wave only when many photons travel through together
Light is detected as particles, but where they land is governed by wave behaviour
Light is purely a wave, and the dots are produced by flaws in the detector
Light is purely made of particles, and the pattern forms as photons collide
questions.explanation: Each photon arrives at one point, which is particle-like, yet the distribution of many arrivals matches the wave interference pattern, even though photons never meet. Neither model alone explains this; light shows both wave and particle properties.
